subject: Coffee & Tea
title: The Penny University
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Penny University.

hook.text: In 1652, the first coffeehouse opened in London. For a penny, you got coffee and access to conversation.

buildup.text: People called them 'penny universities'—a cup admitted anyone to hear and debate the ideas of the day.

discovery.text: Merchants, scientists, writers, and politicians mixed freely. Social rank mattered less than the quality of your argument.

twist.text: King Charles II tried to close them in 1675, calling them 'seminaries of sedition.' Public outcry reversed the ban in 11 days.

climax.text: The penny university model spread across Europe—coffee as a ticket to knowledge, not just a drink.

punchline.text: One penny, one cup, unlimited debate. Education never cost less.

quiz.question: Why were early London coffeehouses called 'penny universities'?
options: A penny bought coffee and access to intellectual conversation

details.summary: London coffeehouses in the 1600s were called penny universities because for a penny admission and a cup of coffee, anyone could sit and listen to scholars, merchants, and thinkers debate. This democratized access to ideas and information across class boundaries at a transformative moment in history.
details.whyItMatters: The penny university concept shows how affordable caffeine-fueled gathering spaces can accelerate the spread of knowledge and break down social barriers.
takeaways: One penny bought entry and a cup of coffee
Men of all classes could listen to and join debates
Coffeehouses democratized access to ideas and information

faq.question: Who actually attended the penny universities?
faq.answer: Merchants, lawyers, scholars, writers, sailors, and tradespeople all mingled. Social rank mattered less inside a coffeehouse than outside. The rule was that any man could sit at any table and enter any conversation, regardless of his station. Women were excluded.

faq.question: What topics were discussed at penny universities?
faq.answer: Everything: trade and shipping news, scientific discoveries, political events, philosophical ideas, and commercial opportunities. Specific coffeehouses attracted specific crowds. Scientists gathered at one, merchants at another, writers at a third. Information flowed freely.
